claims.claim: cProfile showed 0.037 s cumulative for a pure-Python sum of squares over 200,000 numbers and 0.002 s for NumPy; tracemalloc peak for one million float64 values was 8.0 MB.
claims.source: Run on Python 3.11 with NumPy 2.4.6 in this repository.

concept_html:
Most slow data code spends its time in one or two places, and they are rarely where you guess. Measure first, change one thing, measure again. All tools here are in the Python standard library.

Profile to find where time goes. cProfile counts calls and time per function:

import cProfile, pstats
cProfile.run("main()", "profile.out")
pstats.Stats("profile.out").sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(10)

Sort by cumulative to see which of your functions, including everything they call, takes longest. In this course's build, a job calling a pure-Python sum of squares and a NumPy version over 200,000 numbers showed 0.037 s cumulative for the Python one and 0.002 s for NumPy. In a notebook, %prun main() does the same.

Time a candidate change with timeit. timeit.repeat(fn, repeat=5, number=100) returns five totals, each for 100 calls. Report the minimum divided by number: other processes can only slow a run down, so the fastest run is the best estimate of the code's own cost. Use time.perf_counter(), not time.time(), for manual timing.

Measure memory when that is the limit. tracemalloc reports current and peak allocation: one million float64 values showed a peak of 8.0 MB, as expected at 8 bytes each. For pandas, df.memory_usage(deep=True) counts the contents of text columns, not just the pointers.

Rules:

  • Profile with realistic data sizes. A 100-row sample hides what dominates at 10 million rows.
  • Keep setup out of the timed region: reading files, building inputs, copying frames.
  • Fix the biggest cost first. Speeding up a function that takes 2% of the runtime cannot save more than 2%.
  • Keep a test around the code you optimise (lesson B17-L1), so faster does not become wrong.

def best_time(fn: Callable[[], object], repeat: int = 5, number: int = 10) -> float:
"""Best per-call time in seconds over `repeat` rounds of `number` calls."""
if repeat < 1 or number < 1:
raise ValueError("repeat and number must be at least 1")
best = float("inf")
for _ in range(repeat):
start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(number):
best = min(best, (time.perf_counter() - start) / number)

exercises.solution:
import time
from collections.abc import Callable


def best_time(fn: Callable[[], object], repeat: int = 5, number: int = 10) -> float:
    """Best per-call time over several rounds.

    Args:
        fn: Function to time, called with no arguments.
        repeat: Number of rounds.
        number: Calls per round.

    Returns:
        The smallest per-call time in seconds.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If repeat or number is below 1.
    """
    if repeat < 1 or number < 1:
        raise ValueError("repeat and number must be at least 1")
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(repeat):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(number):
            fn()
        best = min(best, (time.perf_counter() - start) / number)
    return best

title: Measure before you optimise
why_html: An analyst spent two days rewriting a weighting function in Numba because "loops are slow in Python". The job still took 40 minutes. A profile, run afterwards, showed 36 of those minutes in reading 300 CSV files one at a time with default type inference. Switching to one Parquet read with explicit dtypes cut the job to 5 minutes. The Numba rewrite saved 20 seconds.
